new_statements.rule_in_words: Native words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic (presyllable + main syllable); stress always falls on the main syllable, which is word-final; the optional presyllable (Ca/Cu/Ci or a syllabic nasal) is unstressed with reduced vowel contrasts. Corroborated first-hand for individual [brv] communities by Theraphan 1980:222 (Woen Buek/Khong Chiam: 'Main syllables.. always receive stress', disyllables = presyllable + main syllable) and Tebow 2010:16 (Khok Sa-at: 'The first syllable of disyllabic words is always unstressed.. The major syllable is always stressed'). Register language, no tones (Tebow 2010:15; Theraphan 1980:224).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Miller & Miller 1995, Theraphan 1980 and Tebow 2010 say nothing about secondary stress. Jungprasert 1986:26 (Dong Luang, after Darunee 1986) distinguishes 'minor syllables' C(C)V(C) that 'take secondary stress' (e.g. /kiska:j?/ 'lazy') from Ca/N presyllables that are 'always unstressed'.
new_statements.exceptions: None for native words. Tebow & Lew 2013:129-130 note compounds and Thai/Lao loanwords of up to four syllables and /s/-initial loans whose first-syllable vowel is not reduced; no stress rule is given for these.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the phonological word (maximally presyllable + main syllable) in citation/elicited forms; Miller & Miller's statement is made jointly for five Bru communities of NE Thailand (all under Ethnologue [brv]) plus So of Kusuman.
new_statements.identity_note: Miller & Miller 1995 state the rule jointly for six NE-Thailand Katuic communities: five Bru villages (Woen Buek/Khong Chiam, Ubon; Dong Sen Kew/Chanuman; Dong Luang and Rom Klaw, Mukdahan; Khok Sa-at/Phang Khon, Sakon Nakhon) that all fall under Ethnologue's Western Bru [brv] = west2397, plus So of Kusuman (sooo1254). Corroborating single-variety statements: Theraphan 1980 = Bruu of Woen Buek (Khong Chiam), which Gehrmann 2016:22 n.12 regards as typologically Eastern Bru although Glottolog/Ethnologue file it under west2397; Tebow 2010 and Tebow & Lew 2013 = Bru Khok Sa-at / 'Bru Sakon Nakhon' (uncontroversially Western Bru); Jungprasert 1986 = 'So (Bru)' of Dong Luang (Western Bru per Gehrmann's Table 32, though Glottolog files the Dong Luang 'So' theses under sooo1254). Wheeler 2022 (Glottolog's top-ranked west2397 grammar) describes Bru of Nakai District, Khammouane, Laos, a different upland community.

sources.note: sec.2.4 surveys phonologies of Bru varieties (Khong Chiam pp.28-29, So Kusuman, Bru Dong Luang etc.); p.76: minor syllables are in 'unstressed position in the canonical WK word' (general West Katuic). p.22 n.12: Khong Chiam Bru is 'typologically.. sources.note: p.16 (p.31), sec.2.1 Phonology (based on a 3000-word dictionary of Bru Khok Sa-at, Sakon Nakhon): 'Phonological words are mainly monosyllabic or disyllabic. The first syllable of disyllabic words is always unstressed and restricted to three types.. The major syllable is always stressed'. p.15: 'two registers, but no tones'.

sources.citation: Miller, John D. & Carolyn P. Miller. 1995 (sealang footer (c)1994). Notes on phonology and orthography in several Katuic Mon-Khmer groups in Northeast Thailand. Mon-Khmer Studies 24: 27-51.
sources.note: p.45 sec.5.1 'Main syllable': all six NE-Thailand dialects studied (Bru of Woen Buek/Khong Chiam, Dong Sen Kew/Chanuman, Dong Luang, Rom Klaw/Nikhom Khamsoi, Khok Sa-at/Phang Khon, plus So of Pho Thi Phai San/Kusuman) have 'a sesquisyllabic structure.. in which a non-stressed non-obligatory pre-syllable is followed by a stressed obligatory main syllable'. sec.5.2 pp.45-46: presyllable vowel a/u/i, length non-contrastive there.

sources.citation: Chollada Jungprasert. 1986. Clauses in So (Bru) of Dong Luang, Mukdahan Province. MA thesis, Mahidol University.
sources.note: Ch.I 'Brief sketch of Dong Luang So phonology' (pp.20-28, stated to be mostly taken from Darunee Kulachol 1986): p.25 'A major syllable is defined as a syllable which always takes primary stress'; p.26 'A minor syllable is defined as a syllable which take[s] secondary stress' (C(C)V(C), e.g. /kiska:j?/ 'lazy'); pp.27-28 presyllables Ca and syllabic nasal 'always unstressed'. Position of the major syllable is shown only by examples (word-final).

sources.citation: Theraphan L. Thongkum. 1980 (often cited 1979). The distribution of the sounds of Bruu. Mon-Khmer Studies 8: 221-293.
sources.note: Bruu of Ban Woen Buek, Khong Chiam, Ubon Ratchathani. p.222 sec.2 'Syllables': 'Main syllables, of the structure C(C)V(C).., always receive stress. The majority of words in Ban Wen Buek Bruu are either monosyllabic (main syllable) or disyllabic (presyllable + main syllable).' Disyllabic examples transcribed with the stress mark before the final syllable (ra'pang 'swamp', ?a'kaa 'fish', sa'wiir 'dizzy'). p.224: register pairs have the same pitch (no tone).
